analysis.one_liner: Authorizes TransCanada to build the Keystone XL oil pipeline from Canada across the U.S.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 252-161 on November 14, 2014, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would hand TransCanada, a Canadian pipeline company, congressional approval to build the Keystone XL pipeline across the U.S.-Canada border, skipping the normal presidential permitting review. It would also declare that the environmental review already done fully satisfies every federal environmental law that applies, including the Endangered Species Act, and channel any court challenges straight to the D.C. federal appeals court. The House passed it in the days after the 2014 midterm elections, but the Senate adjourned without voting on it.
analysis.who_benefits: TransCanada and the Canadian oil sands producers whose crude the pipeline would carry gain most: the bill converts a pending permit application into a direct act of Congress, wipes away remaining environmental-review obligations, and makes court challenges harder to bring. Pipeline construction contractors and Gulf Coast refineries that process heavy crude would also gain, and the project would support thousands of temporary construction jobs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directly authorizes TransCanada Keystone Pipeline, L.P. to build, connect, operate, and maintain the pipeline and cross-border facilities described in its May 2012 application to the State Department, replacing the normal presidential permit process with an act of Congress.

It declares that the State Department's January 2014 environmental impact statement fully satisfies the National Environmental Policy Act and any law requiring federal agency consultation or review, including Endangered Species Act consultation, so no further federal environmental review would be required.
It restricts any legal challenge to the project to direct appeal in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, removing ordinary lower-court and multi-venue challenges.
Pipeline construction would have created thousands of temporary construction jobs, one of the main arguments supporters made on the House floor.

analysis.who_pays: Communities along the pipeline route and the public generally would bear the risk of spills and the consequences of locking in decades of oil sands transport, with the bill short-circuiting the environmental and court review that normally applies. The bill also leaves in place the current exemption that lets oil sands crude skip the 8-cents-per-barrel fee other oil pays into the federal Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities along the route and the public

drawbacks.text: The bill would declare the existing environmental review sufficient under every federal environmental law, including the Endangered Species Act, cutting off the further agency review opponents argued was still needed.

Oil sands crude is currently exempt from the 8-cents-per-barrel contribution to the federal Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund that conventional crude pays; House Democrats offered a motion requiring TransCanada to certify its oil would pay into the fund, and the House rejected it 192-224 along party lines.
All legal challenges would go on direct appeal to the D.C. Circuit with no district-court stage, narrowing the public's access to the courts compared with ordinary projects.
The construction jobs are temporary and most of the oil sands crude would flow to Gulf Coast refineries and export, so the long-term national benefit was disputed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivered a concrete, permanent benefit to one company and the oil sands industry while leaving the public to absorb spill and environmental risk with reduced review and reduced court access. The strongest case for it — temporary construction jobs and heavier crude supply to Gulf refineries — did not address the exemption from spill-fund fees or the procedural shortcuts, and the House rejected the amendment that would have closed the fee exemption.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 252-161 in the post-election lame-duck session, but the Senate received it on November 17 and adjourned on January 3, 2015 without ever voting on it.

narrative.text: The House introduced the bill on November 12, 2014, six days after the midterm elections, and moved it to a floor vote within two days under a rule that closed it to amendments.

Before the passage vote, the House rejected a Democratic motion to recommit 192-224; the motion would have required TransCanada to certify that oil sands crude it shipped would pay into the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund like conventional crude. Every voting Democrat supported the motion and every voting Republican opposed it.
The bill passed the House on November 14, 2014, 252-161 with one present: 221 of 233 voting Republicans in favor, and 31 of 192 voting Democrats in favor.
The Senate received the bill on November 17, 2014, and took no further action on it before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: TransCanada and the oil sands industry are no worse off, since the normal State Department permitting process remained open to them and they avoided a law that would have locked in approval with reduced environmental and court review. Communities along the proposed route and groups seeking stronger spill-fee treatment for oil sands crude avoided the bill's shortcuts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil sands shippers kept the normal review path

for.name: Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it to a House floor vote within two days of introduction.

for.name: 221 of 233 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted for final passage, providing nearly all of the bill's 252 votes, and unanimously opposed the Democratic motion to require oil sands crude to pay into the oil spill trust fund.

for.name: 31 of 192 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Crossed party lines to vote for final passage.

against.name: Lois Capps
against.role: U.S. Representative, ranking member of the Energy and Commerce environment subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit with instructions requiring TransCanada to certify its oil sands crude would pay into the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund; the motion failed 192-224.

against.name: 41 Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Defeated a motion to cut off debate on a companion Keystone XL approval bill (S. 2280) at 59-41 on November 18, 2014, short of the 60 needed; no Keystone bill received a Senate vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed congressional legislation approving the pipeline ahead of his State Department decision, and later rejected the project's permit.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was mostly party line: 221 of 233 voting Republicans and 31 of 192 voting Democrats backed passage, and the spill-fee motion to recommit split entirely by party, 192 Democrats to 224 Republicans.

industries.industry: TransCanada and Canadian oil sands producers
industries.note: The bill would have converted the company's pending permit application into a direct act of Congress, waived remaining environmental review, and made court challenges harder. Its main customers, oil sands producers, would have gained a dedicated route to Gulf Coast refineries while their crude stays exempt from the 8-cents-per-barrel spill-fund fee conventional oil pays.
The project would have meant thousands of temporary construction jobs, which supporters cited as the main benefit for ordinary workers.
Refineries built to process heavy Canadian crude would gain a new supply line; much of the refined product would be positioned for export rather than domestic use.
Railroads currently move a large share of oil sands crude and would lose that traffic to the pipeline, which supporters of both rail and pipeline frame around spill and accident safety trade-offs.
